column2: What exactly does a next-token-prediction model learn — a program, a database of answers, or something else?
column3: A conditional probability distribution over the next token given the previous tokens: \( \pi_\theta(a\mid s) \). Everything else it appears to do is sampling from that distribution.

column2: Why doesn't that training objective already make the model helpful?
column3: Because it only rewards matching the corpus. There is no term in the objective that compares two possible responses and says which is better. The corpus contains cruelty and error as faithfully as it contains kindness and truth, and the model learns to reproduce all of it.

column2: What is the “format” wall that stops us from just using supervised fine-tuning?
column3: Human preference data comes as comparisons, not as demonstrations. A ranking is not a target string, so there is nothing to compute a per-token loss against. Comparisons are cheap and scalable; ideal answers are neither.

column2: What is the “location” wall?
column3: The quality signal is a property of the whole sequence, not of individual tokens. It arrives once, at the end. You cannot assign a per-token label to whether a derivation is correct.

column2: In one line: what is the difference between supervised learning and reinforcement learning?
column3: Supervised learning imitates a label; reinforcement learning optimises a scalar reward obtained by acting in an environment. The second has no dataset of correct actions — only feedback.

column2: What makes a reward “verifiable”, and give the two domains where this works best.
column3: Verifiable means deterministic and mechanically checkable — a test case passes or it doesn't. Mathematics and programming are the two domains, because a checker can grade the outcome without a human, for free, at unlimited scale.

column2: Why is an open-ended chat assistant the hard case?
column3: Because there is no checker. The reward for “was this reply good” is a human judgement, so it must be learned from preference comparisons rather than computed — and the learned reward model becomes the ceiling on how good the assistant can become.

column2: In the Atari framing, what is the “state”, what is the “action”, and where does the “reward” come from?
column3: The state is the current screen (or the things on it), the action is one of the joystick moves, and the reward is the score. The environment — the machine — supplies the next state and the reward.

column2: What does the word “Markov” assert, and what does that force the state to be?
column3: It asserts that the transition kernel depends only on the current state and action: \( p(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t,\dots,s_0)=p(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t) \). So the state must contain everything about the past that matters — for a language model, the whole text so far.

column2: What are the two distinct reasons for the discount factor \( \gamma \)?
column3: (i) Well-posedness: on an infinite horizon the undiscounted sum may diverge, so no finite maximum exists. (ii) Horizon control: \( \gamma \) dials how far ahead the agent optimises.

column2: Write the trajectory distribution, and say which factors depend on \( \theta \).
column3: \( p_\theta(\tau)=\rho_0(s_0)\prod_t\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)p(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t) \). Only the policy factors \( \pi_\theta \) depend on \( \theta \). The initial distribution and the transition kernel are properties of the world.

column2: Why does that factorisation matter so much?
column3: Because when we differentiate with respect to \( \theta \), the two \( \theta \)-free factors differentiate to zero and vanish. The gradient will depend only on the policy — and never on the world's transition rule.

column2: Why is \( \mathbb{E}_{\tau}\big[\nabla_\theta R(\tau)\big] \) useless?
column3: Because \( R(\tau) \) contains no \( \theta \), so its gradient is identically zero. The parameters influence the objective only by changing the distribution over trajectories, never the reward of a given trajectory.

column2: In one phrase: what is being differentiated in \( \nabla_\theta J \)?
column3: The measure — the probability distribution over trajectories — not the integrand.

column2: What does the trick convert the problem into, and why does that help?
column3: It converts the gradient of an intractable integral into an expectation of a computable quantity, \( \mathbb{E}[\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau)R(\tau)] \), which can be estimated by sampling trajectories and averaging.

column2: What does the policy gradient theorem free you from needing, and why is that the difference between theory and practice here?
column3: It removes any dependence on the state-transition distribution \( p(s'\mid s,a) \). For a language model interacting with the world that rule is unknowable — so without this result the whole approach would be unusable.

column2: Name the three things you need in order to run this estimator.
column3: (i) \( \nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta \), free from backprop through the model; (ii) an estimate of the advantage \( \hat A \); (iii) many rollouts — batches of sampled trajectories.

column2: Does subtracting a constant baseline reduce variance?
column3: No. \( \mathrm{Var}(X-c)=\mathrm{Var}(X) \). Variance falls only if the baseline correlates with the return — so it must depend on the state, not be a constant.

column2: What is the difference between \( V^\pi(s) \) and \( Q^\pi(s,a) \), in words?
column3: \( V \) is the expected return from a state, not knowing which action will be taken (averaging over the policy). \( Q \) is the expected return from a state given a particular action. So \( Q \) is \( V \) plus the effect of that action.

column2: Why is \( R_t - V(s_t) \) an estimate of the advantage, and why does it need only one sample?
column3: Because \( \mathbb{E}[R_t\mid s,a]=Q(s,a) \) and \( V(s) \) is constant given \( s \), so the expectation of the difference is \( Q-V=A \). Dropping the expectation from an unbiased estimator leaves a single-sample estimator.

column2: Recite the key equation, and say in one sentence what it instructs you to do.
column3: \( \nabla_\theta J\approx\mathbb{E}[\sum_t\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)\hat A_t] \). Push up the log-probability of actions whose advantage was positive and down those whose advantage was negative, weighted by the size of the advantage.

column2: In the language-model MDP, what are \( s_t \), \( a_t \), and \( \mathcal{A} \)?
column3: \( s_t \) is the entire text so far (prompt plus generated tokens), \( a_t \) is the next token, and \( \mathcal{A}=\mathcal{V} \) is the whole vocabulary — tens of thousands of actions.

column2: When is the reward nonzero, and why does that matter?
column3: Only at the final step, as one number scoring the whole response. It is a sparse terminal reward, which is why the advantage must be estimated from the episode's outcome and why some architectures add a learned value function to help.

column2: What does “on-policy” mean, and what specifically does it cost you?
column3: The expectation is over trajectories from the policy currently being optimised. So every update needs freshly generated rollouts — for an LLM, full inference on the model being trained, which is the dominant cost.

column2: Why is a transformer an unusually good place to use importance sampling?
column3: Because it is an explicit likelihood model: the log-probability of the sampled token under the old policy was recorded, and the current model can recompute it in one forward pass. The importance ratio \( \pi_\theta/\pi_{\text{old}} \) is therefore cheap and exact.

column2: Why does the surrogate objective blow up when the policy moves too far?
column3: Because the importance ratio \( \pi_\theta/\pi_{\text{old}} \) is unbounded. Far from \( \theta_{\text{old}} \) it multiplies the advantage by a huge factor, so the objective — and its gradient estimate — becomes enormous and high-variance.

column2: What is TRPO's constraint, in words and in symbols?
column3: Keep the new policy inside a trust region around the old one: maximise the surrogate subject to \( \mathbb{E}_s[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\text{old}}(\cdot\mid s)\|\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s))]\le\delta \).

column2: Write the PPO clipped objective from memory. What is \( \epsilon \) roughly?
column3: \( L^{\text{CLIP}}=\mathbb{E}_t[\min(r_t\hat A_t,\mathrm{clip}(r_t,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat A_t)] \), with \( \epsilon\approx 0.1 \) to \( 0.2 \).

column2: Why \( \min \) rather than \( \max \)?
column3: \( \min \) is the pessimistic choice: it flattens the objective once you have moved far in a beneficial direction (so you stop), but keeps it steep when you have moved far in a harmful direction (so you keep correcting). A \( \max \) would let the policy run away.

column2: With \( r=1.2 \), \( \epsilon=0.1 \) and \( \hat A=+0.8 \), which term does the \( \min \) choose, and what does that imply about the gradient?
column3: The clipped term, \( 1.1\times0.8=0.88 < 0.96 \). The objective is locally constant there, so the gradient with respect to that move is zero — no further reward for increasing the probability.

column2: Why are pairwise preferences easier to collect than absolute scores?
column3: Because a comparison cancels the rater's private calibration. Two people will disagree about whether a reply is a 6 or a 9, but agree far more reliably about which of two replies is better. Comparing is also a cheaper cognitive task than authoring or grading.

column2: Write the Bradley–Terry model and its training objective.
column3: \( P(y_w\succ y_l\mid x)=\sigma(r_\phi(x,y_w)-r_\phi(x,y_l)) \), fitted by maximising \( \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\log\sigma(r_\phi(x,y_w)-r_\phi(x,y_l))] \).

column2: Which pairs does the reward-model loss concentrate on, and why?
column3: The ones the model currently ranks wrongly. A correctly-ranked pair gives \( \sigma\approx1 \) and \( \log\sigma\approx0 \), so almost no gradient; a reversed pair gives a large gradient.

column2: Why is a Bradley–Terry reward only defined up to a per-prompt constant?
column3: Because the model depends only on \( r(x,y_w)-r(x,y_l) \), and both responses share the same \( x \). Adding any function of \( x \) alone — in particular a constant — cancels in the difference and leaves the likelihood unchanged. So only differences between responses to the same prompt are identifiable.

column2: Name two things Bradley–Terry fails to represent.
column3: Ties (it forces a strict winner), and any preference that cannot be expressed as a logistic function of a single scalar difference between two responses.

column2: What is reward hacking, in one sentence?
column3: The optimiser finds inputs that score highly under the learned reward model while being worse by actual human preference — it exploits the proxy's errors rather than the thing the proxy was meant to measure.

column2: What is the standard mitigation, and what does its strength parameter trade off?
column3: A KL penalty to the frozen reference policy, \( -\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\text{ref}}) \). Small \( \beta \): chases the reward and hacks it. Large \( \beta \): stays near the reference and barely improves.

column2: What is the closed-form optimum of the KL-regularised reward objective, and in words, what is it?
column3: \( \pi^\star(y\mid x)=\frac{1}{Z(x)}\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp(r(x,y)/\beta) \). It is the reference model re-weighted by an exponential tilt toward high reward, with \( \beta \) controlling how sharp the tilt is.

column2: Why does the partition function \( Z(x) \) cancel in DPO? Be precise.
column3: Because \( Z(x) \) depends only on the prompt \( x \), and the preferred and rejected responses are answers to the same prompt. It therefore appears twice in the reward difference with identical value and subtracts to zero.

column2: What would break if the two responses came from different prompts?
column3: \( Z(x_w)\neq Z(x_l) \) in general, so the terms would not cancel, and you would be back to needing to compute an intractable normaliser. DPO's derivation requires a shared prompt.

column2: Write the DPO loss and define the implicit reward.
column3: \( \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}=-\mathbb{E}[\log\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_l))] \) with \( \hat r_\theta(x,y)=\beta\log(\pi_\theta(y\mid x)/\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)) \).

column2: Is DPO reward-free? What value does the loss take at initialisation, and why?
column3: Not quite — the reward is implicit, \( \beta\log(\pi_\theta/\pi_{\text{ref}}) \); what is gone is the reward network and the RL loop. At init the loss is exactly \( \ln 2\approx0.693 \) because every log-ratio is zero, so the sigmoid is \( \tfrac12 \).

column2: In GRPO, what replaces the value function as the baseline, and what does it require?
column3: The mean reward of a group of \( G \) sampled answers to the same prompt, normalised by the group's standard deviation. It requires a verifiable reward, since there is no learned reward model.

column2: Name the two outright mathematical errors in the source.
column3: (i) The claim that subtracting a constant baseline reduces variance — it does not, \( \mathrm{Var}(X-c)=\mathrm{Var}(X) \). (ii) Writing the return without \( \gamma^t \) after introducing \( \gamma \). (The “grad descent” label is a sign/word mismatch rather than a mathematical error.)

column2: State the two structural observations that the whole essay rests on.
column3: (i) In \( p_\theta(\tau)=\rho_0\prod_t\pi_\theta\,p \), only the policy factor depends on \( \theta \) — which yields the policy gradient theorem. (ii) A quantity depending only on the prompt cancels in a comparison between responses to that prompt — which yields the DPO cancellation.
